The present invention relates to methods and systems for bi-planar fluoroscopy, such as with dual fluoroscopes mounted to C-arms for lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) fluoroscopy of a patient. In one aspect of the invention, a bi-planar fluoroscopy system may generally include first and second fluoroscopes. In general, each fluoroscope may be positioned and aimed to provide different viewing angles and/or orientations of the target, such as, for example, placement for lateral and AP views of the target. In some exemplary embodiments, both fluoroscopes may be maintained as “fixed or locked” in AP and lateral positions, respectively, for example, and then each controlled by a set of proximally located control mechanisms, such as one control mechanism (e.g. a foot pedal or voice command specific to operation of a given fluoroscope each). The control mechanisms may further be adapted for use by a single operator individually and/or simultaneously. This may be particularly desirable for spinal procedures, such as for pedicle screw or kyphoplasty balloon placement, and may provide significantly enhanced efficiency and time reduction for these procedures, by completely negating subsequent movements after initial AP and lateral positions have been fixed with C-arms locked into such positions.

outputs.L1:
The present invention relates to methods and systems for bi-planar fluoroscopy, such as systems employing dual fluoroscopes mounted on C-arms to provide lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) fluoroscopic imaging of a patient. In one aspect, a bi-planar fluoroscopy system may generally include first and second fluoroscopes. Each fluoroscope may be positioned and oriented to provide different viewing angles and/or orientations of a target, such as, for example, placement to obtain lateral and AP views of the target.

In certain exemplary embodiments, both fluoroscopes may be maintained in “fixed” or “locked” AP and lateral positions, respectively, and each fluoroscope may be controlled by a set of proximally located control mechanisms, such as a dedicated control mechanism for each fluoroscope (e.g., a foot pedal or voice command specific to operation of a given fluoroscope). The control mechanisms may further be adapted for use by a single operator, either individually and/or simultaneously.

This configuration may be particularly desirable for spinal procedures, such as pedicle screw placement or kyphoplasty balloon placement, and may provide significantly enhanced efficiency and reduced procedure time by eliminating the need for subsequent movements after the initial AP and lateral positions have been established and the C-arms locked into those positions.
outputs.L2:
The invention concerns techniques and equipment for bi-planar fluoroscopy, including arrangements in which two fluoroscopes are mounted on C-arms to obtain lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) images of a patient. In one embodiment, a bi-planar fluoroscopy apparatus can broadly comprise a first fluoroscope and a second fluoroscope. Each fluoroscope may be oriented and directed so that the target can be viewed from distinct angles and/or perspectives, such as positioning one unit for a lateral image and the other for an AP image.

In certain example configurations, the two fluoroscopes may remain fixed or locked in their respective AP and lateral locations. Operation of each fluoroscope may then be managed through corresponding control devices positioned near the operator, such as separate controls for each fluoroscope, including a foot pedal or a voice-command function assigned to that fluoroscope. These controls may be configured so that a single user can operate them either separately or at the same time.

Such an arrangement can be especially useful during spinal procedures, including pedicle screw placement or positioning of kyphoplasty balloons. It may greatly improve procedural efficiency and shorten operating time by eliminating the need to reposition the fluoroscopes after the initial AP and lateral views have been established and the C-arms have been locked in place.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to bi-planar fluoroscopy systems used to obtain multiple fluoroscopic images of a patient from different viewing angles. In particular, the system may include two fluoroscopes, each mounted on a respective C-arm, so that the fluoroscopes can be arranged to provide different views of an anatomical region during a medical procedure.

In one example, a first fluoroscope may be positioned to obtain a lateral view of the patient, while a second fluoroscope may be positioned to obtain an anterior-posterior (AP) view. The two fluoroscopes may therefore provide complementary imaging planes, allowing a physician or other operator to visualize the relevant anatomy from two different perspectives without repeatedly moving a single fluoroscope between positions.

In some embodiments, after the fluoroscopes are initially positioned relative to the patient, both fluoroscopes may be locked or otherwise secured in fixed positions. For example, one fluoroscope may be locked in an AP orientation and the other fluoroscope may be locked in a lateral orientation. Once secured, the fluoroscopes can remain in these positions throughout all or part of the procedure, thereby maintaining consistent imaging angles and reducing the need for repeated alignment.

Each fluoroscope may be controlled using mechanisms located near the operator. Such control mechanisms may include, for example, foot pedals, hand controls, voice-command systems, or other user interfaces. The controls may allow a single operator to activate the first fluoroscope, the second fluoroscope, or both fluoroscopes as needed. In certain embodiments, the operator may acquire images from the fluoroscopes individually or simultaneously, depending on the requirements of the procedure.

The system is particularly useful in spinal procedures, where both AP and lateral visualization are commonly required. By permitting both views to be established at the beginning of the procedure and maintained thereafter, the system can reduce or eliminate the need to reposition C-arms during the operation. This may decrease procedure time, improve workflow, reduce interruptions, and provide more consistent imaging throughout the intervention.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to a bi-planar fluoroscopic imaging system and method for use during medical procedures, particularly procedures requiring accurate placement of instruments or implants within a patient. In one embodiment, the system includes two fluoroscopes, each mounted on a respective C-arm, and positioned to provide different imaging views of the same anatomical region. For example, one fluoroscope may be arranged to obtain a lateral view while the other is arranged to obtain an anterior-posterior view. Other angular orientations may also be used depending on the procedure and the anatomy being treated.

During a procedure, the two C-arm-mounted fluoroscopes may be positioned and locked in fixed locations relative to the patient. Once the desired imaging planes have been established, the fluoroscopes need not be repeatedly moved or repositioned to alternate between views. Instead, the operator can selectively activate either fluoroscope, or both fluoroscopes, as needed. Control may be provided through proximal or hands-free mechanisms, such as foot pedals, hand controls, switches, voice commands, or another suitable user interface located near the operating physician or other operator.

The system allows a single operator to obtain images from two distinct planes without requiring repeated manual repositioning of a fluoroscope or the assistance of multiple imaging technicians. For example, the operator may depress one foot pedal to obtain a lateral image, depress another foot pedal to obtain an anterior-posterior image, or activate both fluoroscopes to obtain substantially simultaneous images from both planes. The fluoroscopes may also be controlled in sequence, alternately, or according to a programmed imaging protocol. In certain embodiments, image acquisition, display, storage, and synchronization may be coordinated through a control unit connected to both fluoroscopes.

This arrangement is especially useful in spinal procedures, where accurate three-dimensional understanding of instrument position is important. Examples include pedicle screw placement, vertebral augmentation, kyphoplasty balloon placement, biopsy needle placement, and other interventions in which a tool must be advanced through bone or soft tissue while avoiding adjacent neural, vascular, or organ structures. By providing both lateral and anterior-posterior views without requiring repeated C-arm movement, the system can help the physician confirm depth, trajectory, and medial-lateral position more quickly and reliably.

The invention improves procedural efficiency by reducing the time required to acquire multiple fluoroscopic views. It also may reduce interruption of the sterile field, lessen dependence on additional personnel, and minimize delays caused by repositioning imaging equipment. Because both fluoroscopes may remain locked in predetermined positions, the imaging geometry can remain consistent throughout the procedure, improving repeatability and reducing the risk of positioning error.

In use, the patient is positioned on an operating table, and the two C-arm fluoroscopes are arranged around the patient to provide the desired bi-planar views. After alignment is confirmed, the C-arms are secured or locked in place. The operator then performs the medical procedure while selectively controlling the fluoroscopes using the proximal control mechanisms. Images from one or both fluoroscopes are displayed on one or more monitors, allowing the operator to guide instruments or implants in real time or near real time.

Accordingly, the invention provides a practical and efficient bi-planar fluoroscopy system that enables independent or simultaneous control of two fixed fluoroscopic imaging devices by a single operator. The system is particularly advantageous in spinal interventions and other image-guided procedures where rapid access to multiple imaging planes can improve accuracy, reduce procedure time, and streamline the overall workflow.

**The Power of “The” and “This”**

“The” and “this” are small words, but they play an important role in English. The word **“the”** is used to point to something specific or already known. For example, when we say “the book,” we mean a particular book, not just any book.

The word **“this”** is also used to identify something specific, but it often refers to something close to the speaker or something being mentioned right now. For example, “this idea” means the idea we are discussing at the moment.

Although they are simple, **“the”** and **“this”** help make communication clear. They guide the reader or listener toward the exact person, object, or concept being discussed. Without these words, many sentences would feel incomplete or confusing. In this way, even the smallest words can have great meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style summary describing an invention for a bi-planar fluoroscopy system using two C-arm fluoroscopes fixed in AP and lateral positions and controlled by a single operator.
counterfactuals.output:
## Patent-Style Summary

Disclosed is a bi-planar fluoroscopy system configured to provide substantially simultaneous or selectively alternating anterior-posterior (AP) and lateral fluoroscopic imaging using two C-arm fluoroscopes maintained in respective fixed imaging orientations. The system includes a first C-arm fluoroscope positioned to acquire AP images of a patient anatomy and a second C-arm fluoroscope positioned to acquire lateral images of the same or overlapping anatomy. The first and second C-arm fluoroscopes are mechanically arranged so as to remain in predetermined AP and lateral positions during a medical procedure, thereby reducing or eliminating the need to repeatedly reposition a single fluoroscope between orthogonal views.

The bi-planar fluoroscopy system further includes a unified operator control interface operatively coupled to both C-arm fluoroscopes. The unified operator control interface allows a single operator to control imaging functions of both fluoroscopes, including image acquisition, fluoroscopy activation, image storage, display selection, exposure settings, collimation, magnification, and switching between AP, lateral, and combined imaging modes. In certain embodiments, the control interface is configured as a single foot pedal assembly, hand controller, touchscreen console, sterile-field controller, or combination thereof. The system may include safety interlocks and exposure-management logic to prevent unintended simultaneous radiation emission or to regulate simultaneous emission according to predetermined dose limits.

In one embodiment, the system includes a controller communicatively coupled to the first and second C-arm fluoroscopes and to one or more display devices. The controller coordinates image acquisition and presentation so that AP and lateral images are displayed side-by-side, overlaid with procedural markers, synchronized in time, or selectively enlarged based on operator input. The controller may further store imaging presets associated with particular procedures or anatomical regions, thereby enabling rapid selection of desired AP and lateral imaging parameters.

The fixed AP and lateral configuration permits continuous availability of orthogonal fluoroscopic views during procedures such as orthopedic fixation, spinal instrumentation, trauma surgery, vascular access, interventional pain procedures, and other image-guided interventions. By allowing a single operator to manage both fluoroscopes from a common interface, the system reduces personnel requirements, decreases procedure time, limits interruptions caused by fluoroscope repositioning, and improves procedural workflow. The system also reduces the risk of loss of image alignment between sequential views and may reduce cumulative radiation exposure by minimizing repeated scout imaging and repositioning fluoroscopy.

In certain embodiments, the two C-arm fluoroscopes are mounted on independent mobile bases, a common support platform, ceiling-mounted supports, floor-mounted supports, robotic positioning arms, or a combination thereof. The system may include mechanical or software-based collision avoidance features to maintain safe spacing between the fluoroscopes, the patient support table, surgical instruments, and medical personnel. Position sensors may be provided to verify that the fluoroscopes remain in the desired AP and lateral orientations, and the controller may inhibit image acquisition if a fluoroscope is outside a predetermined positional tolerance.

The invention therefore provides a compact and coordinated bi-planar fluoroscopic imaging arrangement in which two C-arm fluoroscopes are positioned in fixed orthogonal orientations and controlled by a single operator, enabling efficient acquisition of AP and lateral images without repeated manual repositioning of imaging equipment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft the “present invention relates to” section for a medical imaging patent involving dual fluoroscopes for spinal procedures, including foot pedal or voice command controls.
counterfactuals.output:
The present invention relates generally to medical imaging systems and methods for image-guided procedures. More particularly, the present invention relates to fluoroscopic imaging systems configured for use during spinal procedures, including but not limited to spinal injections, vertebral augmentation, decompression, fusion, instrumentation placement, and other diagnostic or therapeutic interventions involving the spine. 

In certain aspects, the present invention relates to a dual-fluoroscope imaging system in which two fluoroscopic imaging devices are positioned to obtain images of a spinal region from different orientations, such as anteroposterior, lateral, oblique, or other selected views, without requiring repeated manual repositioning of a single imaging device. The system may enable a clinician to acquire, display, store, or compare multiple fluoroscopic views during a procedure, thereby facilitating instrument navigation, anatomical localization, and confirmation of device placement.

In further aspects, the present invention relates to control arrangements for coordinating operation of the dual fluoroscopes during a spinal procedure. Such control arrangements may include one or more foot pedals, foot switches, hand controls, voice command interfaces, or combinations thereof, configured to allow a physician or other operator to selectively activate a first fluoroscope, a second fluoroscope, or both fluoroscopes. The controls may further be configured to select imaging modes, adjust imaging parameters, toggle between views, capture still images, initiate video fluoroscopy, or synchronize image acquisition while maintaining a sterile field and minimizing interruption of the procedure.

In still further aspects, the present invention relates to methods of performing spinal procedures using dual fluoroscopic imaging, wherein a first fluoroscope is arranged to obtain a first view of a target spinal anatomy and a second fluoroscope is arranged to obtain a second view of the target spinal anatomy. The method may include controlling image acquisition by foot pedal input, voice command input, or both, and displaying the acquired images to assist in guiding needles, cannulas, implants, screws, probes, or other instruments relative to spinal anatomy.

The present invention also relates to systems and methods for improving workflow, reducing procedure time, reducing radiation exposure associated with repeated repositioning, and enhancing accuracy in spinal interventions by providing selectively controllable, multi-angle fluoroscopic visualization of the spine.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal patent language, describe an embodiment of a dual fluoroscopy setup with first and second fluoroscopes aimed at different viewing angles and independently or simultaneously controlled by proximal controls.
counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a dual fluoroscopy system comprises a first fluoroscope and a second fluoroscope disposed with respect to an examination region such that the first fluoroscope is oriented to acquire images along a first viewing axis and the second fluoroscope is oriented to acquire images along a second viewing axis different from the first viewing axis. The first and second viewing axes may be angularly offset to provide corresponding different fluoroscopic views of an anatomical structure, instrument, implant, or other object positioned in the examination region.

Each of the first and second fluoroscopes may include a respective radiation source and a respective detector positioned to define the corresponding viewing axis. The first fluoroscope may be arranged to obtain, for example, an anteroposterior, lateral, oblique, cranial-caudal, or other desired projection, while the second fluoroscope may be arranged to obtain a different projection relative to the same examination region. The fluoroscopes may be supported by respective movable arms, gantries, C-arms, robotic positioning mechanisms, or other support structures configured to permit positioning and angular adjustment of the fluoroscopes relative to the examination region.

The system further comprises one or more proximal controls operatively coupled to the first and second fluoroscopes. The proximal controls may be located adjacent to, or within reach of, an operator positioned near a patient, procedure table, sterile field, or instrument manipulation site. The proximal controls are configured to permit selective control of the first fluoroscope, the second fluoroscope, or both the first and second fluoroscopes. In particular, the proximal controls may include one or more switches, buttons, triggers, pedals, touch interfaces, joysticks, sliders, rotatable members, voice-activated controls, or other user input devices configured to initiate image acquisition, adjust exposure parameters, change fluoroscopic mode, reposition a fluoroscope, or otherwise control operation of the fluoroscopes.

In certain implementations, the proximal controls are operable in an independent mode in which a first control input actuates or adjusts the first fluoroscope without actuating or adjusting the second fluoroscope, and a second control input actuates or adjusts the second fluoroscope without actuating or adjusting the first fluoroscope. The proximal controls may also be operable in a simultaneous mode in which a single control input actuates or adjusts both the first and second fluoroscopes concurrently. For example, a simultaneous fluoroscopy command may cause both fluoroscopes to acquire images at substantially the same time, thereby providing different-angle fluoroscopic views of the examination region. In other embodiments, the simultaneous command may cause substantially concurrent activation while permitting different exposure parameters, imaging rates, magnification settings, collimation settings, or acquisition durations for the respective fluoroscopes.

A controller may be operatively connected between the proximal controls and the first and second fluoroscopes. The controller may be configured to receive input signals from the proximal controls and, responsive thereto, generate control signals for independently activating the first fluoroscope, independently activating the second fluoroscope, or simultaneously activating both fluoroscopes. The controller may further be configured to coordinate timing of image acquisition, synchronize image capture, prevent unintended overlapping exposures, manage dose limits, store images from each fluoroscope, and display images from the first and second fluoroscopes on one or more displays. The displays may present the images side-by-side, overlaid, sequentially, or in another arrangement suitable for providing the operator with multi-angle visualization.

In use, the first fluoroscope is positioned at a first selected viewing angle relative to an examination region, and the second fluoroscope is positioned at a second selected viewing angle different from the first selected viewing angle. An operator may manipulate an instrument or perform a procedure while using the proximal controls to selectively obtain a first fluoroscopic image from the first viewing angle, a second fluoroscopic image from the second viewing angle, or substantially simultaneous fluoroscopic images from both viewing angles. The ability to control the first and second fluoroscopes independently or simultaneously from proximal controls permits the operator to obtain multi-angle fluoroscopic information without requiring remote operation of separate fluoroscopy controls and without repositioning a single fluoroscope between successive views.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an invention disclosure paragraph for a bi-planar fluoroscopy apparatus that improves surgical efficiency by keeping AP and lateral C-arms fixed after initial positioning.
counterfactuals.output: Disclosed is a bi-planar fluoroscopy apparatus and method for improving surgical workflow by enabling simultaneous setup and maintained positioning of an anteroposterior (AP) C-arm and a lateral C-arm relative to a surgical target. The apparatus includes first and second fluoroscopic imaging arms configured to be independently positioned during an initial alignment step to obtain desired AP and lateral views of the operative anatomy. Once aligned, the AP and lateral C-arms are locked or otherwise maintained in fixed spatial relationship to the patient and/or operating table, permitting repeated acquisition of AP and lateral fluoroscopic images without requiring repositioning, re-draping, or exchange of a single C-arm between views. The system may include coordinated controls, collision-avoidance features, sterile-field-compatible positioning locks, and image acquisition software configured to selectively capture, display, and store AP and lateral images during the procedure. By preserving both imaging planes after initial positioning, the apparatus reduces operative delays, minimizes disruption to the sterile field, decreases radiation exposure associated with repeated repositioning, and improves surgical efficiency and accuracy in procedures requiring frequent confirmation of instrument or implant placement.
